title: More sales, less profit
prompt: A regional meal-preparation business is selling well, but its owner is disappointed with profit. She wants to know what has changed and what to do next.

clarifying_facts.answer: Increase annual operating profit by at least one hundred thousand dollars within the next twelve months.
Both meal ranges and all existing sites are in scope; no acquisition or extra site is planned.
Prices and meal volumes are unchanged versus the comparison year.
The fixed-cost base is unchanged; product-level variable costs are available in the first exhibit.
Food safety and the current service standard cannot be compromised.
All quoted improvements are full-year operating impacts; ignore tax, financing and costs not explicitly stated.

key_buckets: Revenue: price, volume and product mix
Variable cost per meal: ingredients, labor and waste
Fixed operating cost and existing capacity
Implementation: supplier reliability, food safety and service
common_gaps: Assuming strong sales imply strong profit
Using an unweighted cost average across unequal volumes
Counting a supplier saving without the cost of controlling quality

exhibit.title: Annual product economics; volumes and prices are unchanged. Quantities are thousands of meals.
columns: Old variable cost per meal, dollars
Current variable cost per meal, dollars

stages.question: How much annual contribution has been lost because of the higher unit costs, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Rebuild old and current product contribution separately, then subtract.
verification.working: Old contribution = 100 times (10 minus 6) plus 50 times (16 minus 10) = 700 thousand dollars. Current contribution = 100 times (10 minus 7) plus 50 times (16 minus 12) = 500 thousand dollars. Loss = 700 minus 500 = 200 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Applies the unweighted average unit-cost increase to all meals.
Counts only the standard product and omits the premium cost increase.

stages.question: What does the product analysis tell you about where to investigate first?
key_points: Higher variable costs explain the contribution deterioration despite stable sales.
Premium meals lose more contribution per meal, but standard meals have the larger volume.
Investigate supplier input prices, portion control and waste before proposing a volume-led recovery.

stages.question: What practical actions could recover profit without weakening the customer proposition?
strong_ideas: Renegotiate ingredients using verified purchase volumes
Test equivalent approved ingredients through food-safety checks
Reduce preparation waste using batch-level tracking
Improve labor scheduling to match production demand
Simplify low-value product variations
Test selective price changes where customer willingness supports them
probes: Which action would you test first and why?
How would you distinguish an ingredient-price problem from excess waste?

exhibit.title: Supplier recovery offer; unchanged annual volumes, full-year benefits, recurring quality costs included, no other incremental costs.
columns: Extra annual quality cost, thousand dollars

stages.question: What annual operating profit improvement would this offer produce, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Build a gross procurement-saving ledger and deduct both recurring quality-cost lines.
verification.working: Gross saving = 100 times 1 plus 50 times 1 = 150 thousand dollars. Extra annual quality cost = 10 plus 10 = 20 thousand dollars. Net improvement = 130 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Omits recurring quality-control costs.
Deducts only one of the two product-specific quality-cost lines.

recommendation.question: What would you recommend to the owner, and what would you validate before committing?
key_points: The supplier offer can exceed the stated profit-improvement target after recurring quality costs.
Pursue a controlled rollout only after validating ingredient equivalence and safety.
Use the cost bridge to track actual savings separately for standard and premium meals.
Do not describe the offer as recovering the entire historic contribution loss.
risks_and_next_steps: Test allergens, quality and shelf life before approving substitutions
Confirm supplier capacity and enforceable pricing
Track actual waste and labor rather than assuming quoted savings arrive
Keep a fallback supplier during the pilot

follow_up_twist.new_fact: The safety trial finds that the proposed ingredient substitute cannot meet mandatory allergen controls.
what_should_change: Reject this supplier offer despite the attractive modeled savings.
Seek a compliant ingredient or a different cost lever.
The financial target cannot override the non-negotiable safety condition.

title: The busy courier
prompt: A local courier is handling more deliveries, yet its owners say profit has gone backwards. They have asked you to find the cause and propose a practical response.

clarifying_facts.answer: Restore at least the prior year annual operating profit without reducing delivery quality.
Standard and express deliveries are the only two services.
The central fixed-cost base is unchanged across years.
Contribution is after all delivery-level variable costs; express has a higher contribution.
There is sufficient spare express capacity for the proposed campaign.
The campaign forecast represents genuinely shifted annual deliveries unless later evidence says otherwise; ignore tax and financing.

key_buckets: Revenue and delivery volumes by service
Contribution per delivery and mix
Central fixed costs and support costs
Commercial actions, capacity and execution
common_gaps: Treating volume growth as equivalent to profit growth
Failing to subtract standard contribution when customers upgrade
Confusing a campaign association with incremental customer behavior

exhibit.title: Courier annual contribution before unchanged central fixed costs; express share is the remainder after standard share.

stages.question: What is the signed change in annual contribution, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Recompute standard and express delivery counts, then sum the two category contribution changes.
verification.working: Before: 80 thousand standard deliveries times 2 plus 20 thousand express times 8 = 320 thousand dollars. Now: 108 thousand standard times 2 plus 12 thousand express times 8 = 312 thousand dollars. Signed change = -8 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Keeps the old delivery mix when applying the larger current volume.
Compares standard-delivery contribution only and ignores the shrinking express category.

stages.question: Why can total volume rise while contribution falls?
key_points: The mix shifts toward the lower-contribution standard service.
Express delivery count falls even though total delivery count rises.
The service-level mix is a better immediate diagnostic than total volume alone.

stages.question: How could the courier improve the mix without forcing customers into unsuitable services?
strong_ideas: Target time-sensitive customers with a clear express proposition
Make service reliability and delivery windows visible at booking
Offer trials to customers with demonstrable urgency
Review which customer groups have shifted away from express
Train sales staff to match service to customer need
Use controlled experiments to measure actual upgrades
probes: How would you avoid discounting customers who would already buy express?
Which metric would distinguish profitable mix improvement from volume growth alone?

exhibit.title: Annual express-upgrade campaign; the listed customers otherwise buy standard service. Benefits and support cost cover the same full year.
rows: Additional annual support cost, thousand dollars

stages.question: What is the incremental annual operating profit from the campaign, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Compare express contribution earned with standard contribution forgone and campaign support cash cost.
verification.working: New express contribution = 3 times 8 = 24 thousand dollars. Standard contribution forgone = 3 times 2 = 6 thousand dollars. Incremental profit = 24 minus 6 minus 5 = 13 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Counts all express contribution without subtracting the standard business it replaces.
Ignores the additional annual campaign support cost.

recommendation.question: Would you run the upgrade campaign, and how does it address the original problem?
key_points: A genuinely incremental upgrade campaign can more than offset the contribution decline after support cost.
Pilot it with an untreated comparison group before scaling.
Protect the promised express service standard and verify that spare capacity is real.
Keep investigating why customers originally shifted toward standard service.
risks_and_next_steps: Measure actual standard-to-express switching
Check whether support cost scales with demand
Monitor missed delivery windows and customer complaints
Do not count organic express customers as campaign wins

follow_up_twist.new_fact: A controlled test shows that the customers credited to the campaign would have bought express even without it.
what_should_change: Stop treating their express contribution as incremental.
Do not scale the paid campaign on the original business case.
Focus on genuine service-choice drivers and use the control group to redesign the offer.

title: Repairs across the county line
prompt: An appliance-repair operator is considering serving a neighboring county. The owner thinks the area looks promising and wants your advice on whether to enter.

clarifying_facts.answer: Achieve positive first-year operating profit without exceeding one hundred thousand dollars of committed fixed launch and operating costs.
Only paid household repairs for one appliance category are in scope.
The funnel inputs apply to the first twelve months, not an eventual mature market.
Qualified contractors can supply all modeled jobs at the stated variable cost.
No extra capital expenditure is needed; the quoted fixed cost includes every launch cost.
Assume the business can legally operate in the county unless new information changes that assumption.

key_buckets: Addressable household need and achievable demand
Repair pricing and full entry costs
Contractor capacity and customer service
Legal access and entry execution
common_gaps: Sizing all households instead of relevant appliance owners
Treating total repair demand as attainable sales
Ignoring launch costs or first-year ramp timing

exhibit.title: First-year local repair-demand funnel; each captured repair household books exactly one job.
rows: Owners buying a paid repair this year, percent
Achievable share of those repairs, percent

stages.question: How many repair jobs should the business expect in its first year, as a whole number?

verification.method: Build the eligible-household count, then apply paid demand and captured share sequentially.
verification.working: 80,000 households times 75 percent = 60,000 appliance owners. One fifth buy repair, giving 12,000 jobs, and one quarter are captured. Forecast = 3000 jobs.

common_mistakes.description: Applies repair demand to all households and omits appliance ownership.
Uses all repair demand rather than the share the entrant can capture.

stages.question: What does the funnel tell you about the most important assumption to validate?
key_points: The entrant needs only a share of paid repair demand, not all appliance owners.
Ownership, paid repair incidence and achievable share each affect the forecast.
Capture share and contractor reliability should be validated locally before committing fixed spending.

stages.question: How would you test demand and establish a credible launch?
strong_ideas: Interview recent repair customers about provider choice
Check competitor lead times and service gaps
Run a small service-area advertising test
Prequalify contractors and audit repair quality
Pilot booking slots before committing permanent coverage
Build referral relationships with relevant appliance retailers
probes: What evidence would justify the assumed capture share?
How would you separate genuine demand from low-intent enquiries?

exhibit.title: First-year repair economics; all launch and annual fixed cash costs are included; no additional capex.
columns: All first-year fixed costs, thousand dollars

stages.question: What first-year operating profit would the entry produce, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Rebuild annual revenue, variable cash cost and fixed cash cost as separate dollar ledgers.
verification.working: Revenue = 3,000 times 120 = 360 thousand dollars. Variable cost = 3,000 times 70 = 210 thousand dollars. Profit = 360 minus 210 minus 100 = 50 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Omits the first-year fixed costs.
Treats sales as contribution and ignores variable repair cost.

recommendation.question: Would you enter the county on the current evidence, and under what conditions?
key_points: The modeled first year is profitable and the fixed-cost commitment meets the stated limit.
Recommend a staged entry after confirming paid demand and contractor quality.
Make continued spending conditional on actual bookings, contribution and customer satisfaction.
Avoid presenting the forecast as proof that the market share will be achieved.
risks_and_next_steps: Validate repair incidence and attainable share with a pilot
Confirm contractor availability at the quoted rate
Track first-time fix rates and warranty rework
Check local operating requirements before launch

follow_up_twist.new_fact: The county introduces an exclusive operating franchise, and this business is not eligible for it.
what_should_change: Do not proceed with the direct-entry plan.
Investigate a lawful partnership with the franchise holder or choose another area.
Commercial attractiveness does not remove the new market-access barrier.

title: Own the hub or use a partner
prompt: An industrial tool-service business sees an opportunity in a nearby industrial park. Management is debating whether to build a local hub or use a service partner. How would you advise them?

clarifying_facts.answer: Enter only if first-year operating profit is positive; prefer the better economic route if service quality is equal.
The three listed industrial segments cover the whole target area.
A captured tool needs exactly one service visit during the first year.
Either operating route can handle up to one thousand annual visits at the quoted costs.
Quoted fixed costs include all first-year setup; prices and variable unit costs remain valid throughout that capacity range.
Ignore tax and financing; contract reliability and customer control matter even when profit differs.

key_buckets: Addressable tools, service frequency and attainable demand
Route-specific revenue and variable delivery cost
Setup and fixed operating cost
Capacity, partner control and delivery execution
common_gaps: Averaging segment tool counts without firm weights
Choosing the cheaper unit cost without fixed costs
Assuming a partner is always the best route at larger volumes

exhibit.title: First-year industrial tool-service demand; each captured tool requires one paid service visit.

stages.question: What annual service-visit volume can the entrant capture, as a whole number?

verification.method: Enumerate customer firms within each segment and add their captured tool visits.
verification.working: Operators contribute 30 times 10 times one half = 150 visits. Workshops contribute 20 times 15 times one half = 150. Warehouses contribute 10 times 20 times one half = 100. Total = 400 visits.

common_mistakes.description: Uses the unweighted average tools per firm for all firms.
Omits attainable share and captures the entire market.

stages.question: What would you investigate before trusting the partner operating route?
strong_ideas: Audit service quality using test jobs
Check turnaround commitments and remedies
Verify qualified technician capacity
Agree ownership of customer relationships and data
Review escalation and warranty responsibilities
Negotiate pricing and termination rights for different volumes
probes: Which issue could outweigh a small profit advantage?
How would you protect customers if the partner failed?

exhibit.title: First-year options at the captured volume; both meet service standards and have sufficient capacity. Fixed costs include setup.

stages.question: How much higher is first-year operating profit with the partner than with the owned hub, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Compare the fixed-cost saving with the partner variable-cost disadvantage in a separate profit bridge.
verification.working: Owned hub profit = 400 times (200 minus 80), divided by 1,000, minus 40 = 8 thousand dollars. Partner profit = 400 times (200 minus 140), divided by 1,000, minus 10 = 14 thousand dollars. Partner advantage = 6 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Compares unit contribution only and ignores the different fixed costs.
Counts the fixed-cost saving but ignores the more expensive partner delivery.

stages.question: What does the economics suggest about choosing a route as volume changes?
key_points: The partner is more profitable at the modeled first-year volume.
Its lower fixed cost is offset partly by a higher unit delivery cost.
Higher sustained volume could favor the owned hub, so the choice should not be treated as permanent.

recommendation.question: Which route would you recommend now, and what evidence could change your answer?
key_points: Use the partner for an initial entry, conditional on verified service standards and a workable contract.
The partner has higher first-year operating profit at the captured demand forecast.
Keep the owned-hub option available if contracted volume materially increases.
Track service outcomes and demand rather than committing solely on a cost spreadsheet.
risks_and_next_steps: Validate attainable customer share
Confirm quoted costs over the relevant volume range
Negotiate service-level and customer-data protection
Review route economics as firm demand develops

follow_up_twist.new_fact: A signed take-or-pay contract now guarantees eight hundred service visits each year; all unit costs, fixed costs and capacity limits stay unchanged.
what_should_change: Recalculate both routes at the higher committed volume.
The owned hub now has the stronger operating economics because its lower unit cost outweighs the extra fixed cost.
Reconsider the owned hub if setup and delivery execution can meet the contract.

title: Acquiring customers without growing
prompt: A small business-software provider is spending on customer acquisition, but its chief executive says the customer base feels stuck. The team wants a growth plan that improves economics as well as headline sign-ups.

clarifying_facts.answer: Add at least fifty active customers over the next renewal year without reducing annual operating profit.
There is one annual subscription product, and the opening customer cohort renews once during the modeled year.
The quoted churn applies only to the opening cohort; newly acquired customers do not churn within the period.
Annual customer contribution is after all incremental service costs and excludes the separate retention program cost.
The team can serve the modeled retained and new customers without extra fixed costs.
Assume acquisitions remain unchanged when testing the retention program; ignore tax and financing.

key_buckets: Customer acquisition by channel and cost
Renewal, churn causes and customer experience
Contribution per customer and program economics
Delivery capability and measurement
common_gaps: Equating sign-ups with net customer growth
Applying cohort churn to newly acquired customers
Confusing a percentage-point change with a relative percentage change

exhibit.title: Annual customer bridge; churn applies only to the opening cohort. Newly acquired customers remain active at year-end.

stages.question: What is the net change in active customers at year-end, as a whole number?

verification.method: Rebuild closing retained and new customer counts, then compare with the opening base.
verification.working: Opening-cohort losses = 1,000 times 20 percent = 200 customers. New customers = 200. Net change = 0 customers.

common_mistakes.description: Counts new acquisitions but ignores churn.
Applies the opening-cohort churn rate to opening plus newly acquired customers.

stages.question: What would you tell the chief executive about the current growth engine?
key_points: New acquisitions are being offset by losses from the opening cohort.
Increasing acquisition spending alone could leave the underlying retention issue unresolved.
The diagnosis should separate avoidable churn from customers who no longer need the product.

stages.question: What retention actions would you test before offering blanket discounts?
strong_ideas: Identify churn reasons through exit interviews
Fix onboarding failures in the first usage period
Provide targeted training for low-adoption accounts
Resolve recurring product reliability problems
Use renewal reminders and early account-health signals
Offer service tiers that better fit customer needs
probes: How would you test whether an action really reduces churn?
Why might a discount improve renewal counts but weaken economics?

exhibit.title: Retention program for the same renewal cohort; contribution is earned for a full renewed annual contract. No effect on new acquisitions.
rows: Annual contribution per retained customer, dollars

stages.question: What incremental annual operating profit would the retention program deliver, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Count retained customers separately under baseline and program renewal rates, then price the difference and deduct program cost.
verification.working: Retained customers increase from 800 to 850, a gain of 50. Added annual contribution = 50 times 600 = 30 thousand dollars. Incremental profit = 30 minus 20 = 10 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Omits the annual program cost.
Treats the five-percentage-point churn reduction as a five-percent relative reduction in baseline churn.

recommendation.question: What growth action would you prioritize based on these results?
key_points: Pilot the targeted retention program while maintaining the current acquisition base.
The modeled renewal improvement meets the active-customer growth objective and has positive incremental annual profit.
Use a comparison group to measure causal renewal improvement.
Continue fixing the product and service issues that created avoidable churn.
risks_and_next_steps: Validate the forecast churn reduction
Check that contribution is not reduced by hidden discounts
Track incremental service demands
Separate renewal-cohort outcomes from new customer activity

follow_up_twist.new_fact: A controlled pilot finds no improvement in renewal rates relative to untreated customers.
what_should_change: Do not roll out the paid retention program on the original business case.
Treat the observed benefit as unsupported and investigate why the intervention failed.
Redirect spending toward measured product fixes or other acquisition and retention options.

title: The tempting partner channel
prompt: A household-goods seller has been offered access to a large marketplace. The commercial team expects many more orders, but the finance team is unconvinced. Should the business pursue the partnership?

clarifying_facts.answer: Increase first-year operating profit rather than maximize orders or gross sales.
Direct and partner orders are the only channels in the model.
Some marketplace orders are expected to replace orders customers would otherwise place directly.
Per-order contribution already includes shipping and channel-variable fees; platform and brand commitments are additional fixed costs.
Fulfillment capacity is sufficient, and no extra capex is required.
All annual forecasts and fees refer to the same first year; ignore tax and financing.

key_buckets: Total customer demand and direct-channel displacement
Contribution economics by channel
Additional fixed fees and commercial commitments
Customer ownership, brand control and execution
common_gaps: Calling all marketplace sales incremental
Applying the direct margin to partner orders
Counting a positive contribution bridge as final profit before new fixed fees

exhibit.title: Annual channel forecast; contribution per order is after all channel-variable costs. Orders are thousands.

stages.question: What incremental annual contribution would the partner channel create, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Build total contribution with and without the partner and subtract the two channel portfolios.
verification.working: Without partner: 100 times 5 = 500 thousand dollars. With partner: 70 times 5 plus 80 times 3 = 590 thousand dollars. Incremental contribution = 90 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Counts partner contribution without the direct contribution that is lost.
Values every partner order at the higher direct-channel contribution.

stages.question: How could the business make the partnership more valuable or less risky?
strong_ideas: Negotiate a lower platform commitment
Restrict listings to products with little direct overlap
Use unique bundles to reduce direct-channel substitution
Test a limited geography before a full rollout
Secure customer and performance data where feasible
Negotiate a shorter trial and clear exit rights
probes: Which proposal addresses cannibalization most directly?
What would you measure to distinguish new customers from displaced direct buyers?

exhibit.title: First-year partner economics; lost direct contribution is a real displaced sale. All fees are additional and cover the same year.

stages.question: What is the signed first-year operating profit impact of the partner plan, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Compare partner contribution after its new fixed commitments with the direct contribution it displaces.
verification.working: Partner contribution after platform fee and brand spending = 240 minus 60 minus 40 = 140 thousand dollars. Deduct 150 thousand dollars of displaced direct contribution. Profit impact = -10 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Treats the channel as wholly incremental and omits lost direct contribution.
Omits the required brand-spending commitment.

stages.question: How should the team interpret more orders alongside a negative profit impact?
key_points: Order growth does not prove incremental value.
Direct contribution lost and required channel spending exceed the retained benefit in the current plan.
A partner test is useful only if it can change or validate the economics rather than assume away the shortfall.

recommendation.question: Would you sign the proposed partnership, and what would need to change?
key_points: Do not sign the full annual commitment on the current forecast.
Renegotiate terms or redesign the offer to reduce direct-channel displacement.
Use a controlled, limited test if it can avoid the full fixed commitment.
Require evidence of incremental operating profit rather than relying on gross order volume.
risks_and_next_steps: Validate direct-channel displacement
Check whether fees are cancellable or volume-linked
Review brand control and customer access
Track contribution after all required spending

follow_up_twist.new_fact: An audited test finds no direct-channel cannibalization; partner order volume, contribution per order and all fees stay unchanged.
what_should_change: Rebuild the case without the direct contribution loss.
The unchanged partner business now has positive incremental profit after the stated fees.
A phased rollout becomes attractive if the zero-cannibalization finding and operational capacity hold.

title: A cheaper protective package
prompt: A homewares distributor wants to reduce packaging spending. A supplier says a lighter package could save money, but the operations team worries about returns. How would you assess the proposal?

clarifying_facts.answer: Deliver at least one hundred thousand dollars of recurring annual cash savings and recover setup cash within six months.
The package changes only for the existing shipment volume.
Product protection and customer service must remain at the current accepted standard.
Quality-control costs and setup are separate; the exhibits include every stated incremental cash cost.
Assume an immediate full rollout for the economics, evenly earned monthly savings, and no working-capital or tax effects.
The supplier can handle the existing shipment volume without a volume penalty.

key_buckets: Packaging material and handling cost
Damage, returns and customer experience
Setup cash, recurring cost and payback
Supplier capacity and controlled implementation
common_gaps: Comparing package prices without damage and quality effects
Treating recurring quality-control cost as a one-off
Confusing annual savings with monthly savings in payback

exhibit.title: Packaging proposal; annual shipment volume is unchanged and all quality-control costs are recurring.
rows: Extra annual quality-control cost, thousand dollars

stages.question: What recurring annual cash saving does the proposal produce, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Compare the old full-year packaging ledger with the new packaging and quality-control ledger.
verification.working: Current packaging costs 240 times 3 = 720 thousand dollars. Proposed packaging and quality control cost 240 times 2 plus 60 = 540 thousand dollars. Recurring saving = 180 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Omits the recurring quality-control cost.
Treats the new package cost as the unit saving rather than subtracting it from the old cost.

stages.question: What would you test before replacing the current package?
strong_ideas: Run transit tests for the most fragile products
Measure actual damage and return rates
Test customer unboxing and usability
Check warehouse packing speed and rework
Validate supplier consistency across batches
Keep a limited fallback stock of the existing package
probes: What result would make you reject the proposal despite the savings?
How would you avoid a trial that understates transport damage?

exhibit.title: Simple cash payback; setup is paid immediately, recurring savings are received evenly at each month-end, and discounting is ignored.
rows: Gross annual packaging saving, thousand dollars
Extra annual quality-control cost, thousand dollars
One-time setup cash cost, thousand dollars

stages.question: After how many complete months are the setup costs recovered, as a whole number?

verification.method: Simulate each month-end net cash saving until cumulative cash exactly recovers the upfront setup payment.
verification.working: Net annual saving = 240 minus 60 = 180 thousand dollars. Monthly saving = 180 divided by 12 = 15 thousand dollars. Setup recovery = 60 divided by 15 = 4 complete months.

common_mistakes.description: Uses gross packaging savings and ignores recurring quality-control cost.
Uses the annual saving as if it were a monthly saving, then rounds to a whole recovery month.

stages.question: What does meeting the savings and payback targets tell you, and what does it not tell you?
key_points: The modeled proposal clears both financial gates.
Those gates do not establish that the lighter package protects products adequately.
A staged trial should confirm the commercial and service assumptions before rollout.

recommendation.question: Would you recommend the package change?
key_points: Proceed only after a representative damage and service trial passes.
The modeled recurring savings and setup payback satisfy the financial criteria.
Roll out in stages and compare damage-adjusted savings against a control group.
Retain the old package for products or routes that do not meet the required protection level.
risks_and_next_steps: Measure returns and replacement shipping costs
Confirm supplier consistency and capacity
Validate that packing labor does not increase
Track realized cash savings and setup spending

follow_up_twist.new_fact: The transit trial shows that the lighter package fails the required protection test for the products in scope.
what_should_change: Do not roll out this package as proposed.
Redesign or limit the change to products that can pass the required protection standard.
Rebuild the economic case after including the compliant design and any extra handling.

title: Automation that saves time
prompt: A customer-support center is considering automating routine tickets. The vendor emphasizes hours saved, while the finance team wants a credible cost reduction. Should the center invest?

clarifying_facts.answer: Approve only a project with nonnegative first-year net cash benefit while maintaining current service quality.
Only the routine tickets in the exhibit are automated.
Paid temporary roles can be removed when their work disappears; no severance or extra redeployment cost applies.
Saved productive hours translate into whole removable roles at the stated hours per role.
Licenses, quality audits and setup are cash outflows; ignore tax, depreciation and working-capital changes.
The first year contains twelve full months of labor savings and recurring software costs.

key_buckets: Workload and time truly removed
Conversion of time into avoidable paid staffing
Technology, quality and setup cash costs
Service performance and rollout risk
common_gaps: Calling time saved a cash saving when staffing cannot change
Forgetting the minutes-to-hours conversion
Approving on recurring savings while ignoring the first-year setup payment

exhibit.title: Annual ticket automation; released work can be removed from paid temporary roles with no severance or service impact.
rows: Annual productive hours per paid role
Annual cash cost per paid role, thousand dollars

stages.question: What annual paid labor cost can be avoided, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Rebuild paid-role requirements before and after automation, then price the whole-role difference.
verification.working: Released time = 120,000 times (5 minus 3) = 240,000 minutes, or 4,000 hours. That removes 4,000 divided by 2,000 = 2 paid roles. Annual avoided cost = 2 times 50 = 100 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Fails to convert saved minutes to hours before calculating paid roles.
Assumes all current ticket-handling labor cost disappears.

stages.question: What assumption makes the labor saving a real cash benefit here?
key_points: The released work corresponds to removable paid temporary roles.
An efficiency gain would not automatically save payroll if staffing and hours stayed fixed.
The whole-role and no-severance assumptions should be checked before the project is approved.

stages.question: How would you design an automation trial that protects service quality?
strong_ideas: Limit the trial to clearly defined routine ticket categories
Route uncertain cases to human agents
Measure resolution quality as well as handling time
Audit failed or repeated contacts
Track actual paid staffing reductions separately from theoretical hours
Compare outcomes with a similar untreated ticket group
probes: What would reveal that the tool merely shifts work to another team?
Which error would be a rollout stop condition?

exhibit.title: First-year cash business case; labor avoidance is realizable, all fees are additional and there are no other cash impacts.

stages.question: What is the signed first-year net cash benefit of automation, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Separate recurring net savings from the upfront setup payment and reconcile their first-year cash effect.
verification.working: Recurring net cash saving = 100 minus 45 minus 20 = 35 thousand dollars. First-year net cash benefit = 35 minus 60 = -25 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Excludes the setup payment from the first-year cash decision.
Omits the recurring quality-audit requirement.

recommendation.question: Would you approve the proposed automation under the stated decision rule?
key_points: Do not approve the full project on the current first-year cash terms.
Real labor avoidance is positive, but setup and recurring costs create a first-year cash shortfall.
Negotiate setup terms or test a smaller design rather than treating hours saved as sufficient evidence.
Keep service quality and the staffing-removal assumption as approval conditions.
risks_and_next_steps: Confirm actual removable paid roles
Check license and audit obligations
Validate first-year timing and implementation effort
Use a controlled service-quality pilot

follow_up_twist.new_fact: The vendor waives the entire one-time setup payment in a binding contract; all other assumptions remain unchanged.
what_should_change: The first-year cash gate is now met by the positive recurring net saving.
Reconsider a phased investment if service quality and paid-role removal are validated.
Keep monitoring recurring license and quality costs rather than assuming the waiver fixes every risk.

title: A price rise with fewer orders
prompt: A maker of specialist storage products wants to raise prices after leaving them unchanged for years. Sales expects some customers to leave. How would you decide whether the increase is sensible?

clarifying_facts.answer: Improve annual operating profit without changing product quality or fixed operating cost.
One product and one proposed price change are in scope.
The sales forecasts represent annual customer response at each quoted price.
Variable cost per item is unchanged; no extra marketing or implementation cost applies in the quantified comparison.
Capacity is sufficient for either volume, so there is no rationing effect.
The forecasts are estimates and should be validated by a controlled price test.

key_buckets: Willingness to pay and customer volume response
Unit contribution at each price
Portfolio and competitive effects outside the single-product model
Testing, communication and implementation
common_gaps: Using revenue growth as the profit test
Assuming volume is unchanged after a price rise
Dividing a contribution target by price rather than margin

exhibit.title: Annual price test; the forecast is for a full year. Variable cost per unit and fixed costs are unchanged.

stages.question: What would be the change in annual contribution, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Reconcile the change in revenue and the change in variable cost as separate dollar effects.
verification.working: Current contribution = 100 times (10 minus 4) = 600 thousand dollars. Proposed contribution = 85 times (12 minus 4) = 680 thousand dollars. Change = 80 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Uses the change in revenue instead of contribution.
Applies the higher price to all current volume and ignores the demand reduction.

stages.question: What would you test or communicate before rolling out the new price?
strong_ideas: Test by comparable customer cohorts where commercially feasible
Interview lost customers about their alternatives
Explain product value rather than only higher costs
Review contract notice periods and renewal timing
Monitor competitor response and cross-product switching
Predefine a contribution and retention decision rule
probes: Which metric would tell you the test is succeeding?
How would you avoid confusing seasonality with price response?

exhibit.title: Contribution-preserving volume floor; fixed costs are unchanged. Units are whole items and all contribution figures cover one year.
rows: Proposed selling price per unit, dollars

stages.question: What minimum annual sales volume preserves the current contribution at the proposed price, as a whole number of units?

verification.method: Accumulate per-unit contribution one unit at a time until it first reaches the current contribution target.
verification.working: New unit contribution = 12 minus 4 = 8 dollars. Required volume = 600,000 divided by 8 = 75000 units. One fewer unit falls short by 8 dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Divides the contribution target by selling price rather than unit contribution.
Uses the old unit contribution of six dollars instead of the proposed unit contribution.

stages.question: How does the break-even volume help you interpret the proposed demand forecast?
key_points: The forecast volume is above the contribution-preserving floor.
There is room for some demand loss, but not unlimited loss.
The contribution threshold offers a clearer rollout gate than revenue or customer count alone.

recommendation.question: What would you recommend on price, and how would you control the risk?
key_points: Run a controlled increase rather than assuming the forecast is certain.
The modeled price and volume combination improves contribution with unchanged fixed costs.
Use the verified contribution-preserving volume as a practical test threshold.
Monitor customer mix, complaints and competitive response before wider rollout.
risks_and_next_steps: Validate actual annualized volume response
Check that unit cost remains unchanged
Watch for spillovers to other products
Avoid assuming an initially favorable response persists indefinitely

follow_up_twist.new_fact: The pilot now indicates annual sales of only seventy thousand units at the higher price, with the same unit cost.
what_should_change: Do not roll out the price increase on this evidence.
The revised volume is below the verified contribution-preserving floor.
Retest price levels, customer groups or value communication before accepting the loss.

title: Quiet hours at the climbing center
prompt: A climbing center is crowded in the evening and quiet during the day. Management proposes a daytime discount to fill the space. They want your view before changing the price list.

clarifying_facts.answer: Increase annual operating contribution using existing capacity while protecting the customer experience.
Peak and off-peak capacity are separate; unused daytime capacity cannot relieve the evening limit.
The discount forecast adds the stated visits without shifting peak demand.
The initial proposal discounts all off-peak visits, including customers who would otherwise pay full price.
Variable visit cost is unchanged, and all other operating costs are fixed for this comparison.
Demand response is a forecast to validate, not a proven effect of the discount.

key_buckets: Capacity and demand by time window
Price response from genuinely additional visits
Price reduction on existing customer demand
Offer eligibility, customer experience and testing
common_gaps: Applying average utilization to every time window
Assuming spare capacity guarantees profitable demand
Ignoring the discount given to customers who already buy

exhibit.title: Annual capacity and paid visits by time window; visits are thousands and capacity cannot be shifted between windows.

stages.question: How many additional off-peak visits could fit within current capacity, as a whole number?

verification.method: Enumerate the unused off-peak visit slots between occupied volume and the off-peak limit.
verification.working: Off-peak capacity is 100 thousand visits and paid visits are 40 thousand. Spare off-peak capacity = (100 minus 40) times 1,000 = 60000 visits.

common_mistakes.description: Treats the whole off-peak capacity as available instead of subtracting existing visits.
Applies overall average utilization to off-peak and rounds down to whole visits.

stages.question: Does spare daytime capacity by itself justify a blanket discount?
key_points: Spare capacity makes additional visits operationally possible.
It does not establish willingness to pay or the incremental profit of the offer.
The economics must include any discount applied to existing customers.

stages.question: How could the center attract profitable daytime use without broadly cutting existing prices?
strong_ideas: Target first-time daytime customers with eligibility checks
Offer limited corporate or school daytime sessions
Create off-peak introductory courses
Use advance bookings for otherwise empty slots
Test bundles that add value instead of only cutting price
Prevent discounted access from spilling into peak hours
probes: Which idea best protects existing full-price demand?
How would you test whether discounted visitors are truly incremental?

exhibit.title: Proposed off-peak offer; the lower price applies to every existing and new off-peak visit. No change to peak visits or other costs.
rows: Variable cost per off-peak visit, dollars

stages.question: What is the signed annual contribution change from the blanket off-peak discount, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Value contribution from the new visits, then subtract the price reduction on all existing off-peak visits.
verification.working: New-visit contribution = 10 times (12 minus 4) = 80 thousand dollars. Price reduction on existing visits = 40 times (20 minus 12) = 320 thousand dollars. Change = -240 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Counts new visitors but ignores the price cut for existing customers.
Reports the revenue change without subtracting variable costs on additional visits.

recommendation.question: Would you recommend the blanket discount, and what alternative would you pursue?
key_points: Reject the blanket off-peak discount on the current contribution forecast.
The price cut for existing visitors outweighs contribution from added visits.
Test a tightly fenced offer or a different off-peak proposition.
Measure incremental contribution and customer switching rather than occupancy alone.
risks_and_next_steps: Validate forecast new demand
Audit discount eligibility and misuse
Track peak-to-off-peak shifting if it occurs
Include any new staffing or marketing cost before scaling

follow_up_twist.new_fact: Booking technology can restrict the discounted offer to verified new off-peak customers, with no price or volume change for existing customers and no extra system cost.
what_should_change: Rebuild the offer without discounting existing demand.
A targeted test now has positive incremental contribution under the unchanged new-visit forecast.
Prioritize eligibility controls and causal demand measurement before scaling.

title: A promising thermal jug
prompt: A reusable-drinkware producer is considering a thermal jug. Customer research is encouraging, and the commercial team wants to launch quickly. The chief executive wants an independent recommendation.

clarifying_facts.answer: Launch only if the first full year has positive incremental operating profit after all capacity and launch costs.
Some jug buyers would otherwise buy an existing product; both use the same production line.
Unit contribution excludes shared fixed launch spending and any extra capacity cost.
The capacity exhibit already includes minutes freed by the displaced existing products; do not add them again.
Demand, contribution and capacity estimates refer to the same first full year; ignore tax, depreciation and financing.
Any production partner must meet the current quality and delivery standard.

key_buckets: Customer need, willingness to pay and attainable demand
Portfolio contribution and product substitution
Launch spending and shared capacity economics
Quality, execution and commercial validation
common_gaps: Counting all new sales as incremental
Adding freed line minutes twice
Approving the product before pricing the bottleneck capacity

exhibit.title: First-year new-product forecast; contribution is after unit-variable cost. Fixed launch costs exclude any extra capacity cost.
rows: New product contribution per unit, dollars
Existing product contribution per unit, dollars
First-year fixed launch cost, thousand dollars

stages.question: Before additional capacity costs, what is the first-year launch operating profit impact, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Compare new-product contribution after launch spending with the existing-product contribution it displaces.
verification.working: New contribution = 40 times 8 = 320 thousand dollars. Lost existing contribution = 10 times 5 = 50 thousand dollars. Profit impact before capacity = 320 minus 50 minus 200 = 70 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Ignores cannibalized existing-product contribution.
Ignores fixed launch spending.

stages.question: What would you test before committing to a full launch?
strong_ideas: Use a limited customer pre-order test
Measure substitution from existing products
Validate willingness to pay at the planned price
Run line trials to confirm production minutes
Get comparable quotes for qualified overflow capacity
Test product quality and delivery lead times
probes: Which test could most change the economics?
How would you distinguish a genuinely new buyer from a buyer switching products?

exhibit.title: Shared-line capacity correction; free minutes include minutes released by displaced existing products. Overtime is available without other costs.
rows: Launch profit before extra capacity, thousand dollars
New product output, thousands of units
Line minutes required per new unit
Cash cost per overtime line minute, dollars

stages.question: After paying for required overtime capacity, what is the signed first-year launch profit impact, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Allocate free line minutes first, price only the uncovered minutes and deduct that cash cost from the pre-capacity profit.
verification.working: Required line time = 40 times 2 = 80 thousand minutes. Free time covers 60 thousand, leaving 20 thousand overtime minutes. Overtime costs 20 times 4 = 80 thousand dollars. Adjusted profit = 70 minus 80 = -10 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Treats a positive product business case as final and ignores extra capacity cost.
Charges overtime for every new line minute instead of using available free capacity.

stages.question: How does the capacity correction change the launch decision?
key_points: The attractive pre-capacity result does not survive the required overtime cost.
Shared-line minutes have a real opportunity or cash cost.
The decision should compare a smaller launch, lower capacity cost or a revised product design rather than ignore the constraint.

recommendation.question: Would you approve the launch at the proposed scale?
key_points: Do not approve the full launch under the current overtime economics.
A positive pre-capacity case is insufficient when the bottleneck correction makes the total impact negative.
Explore qualified lower-cost capacity, product redesign or a smaller pilot.
Revalidate cannibalization and customer demand before fixing the launch scale.
risks_and_next_steps: Confirm true line minutes and available capacity
Avoid counting freed minutes twice
Validate partner quality and delivery
Check fixed launch commitments before reducing scale

follow_up_twist.new_fact: An approved production partner offers all required overflow time at one dollar per line minute, with no setup cost or quality change; every other assumption is unchanged.
what_should_change: Rebuild the case using the lower cost for only the uncovered production minutes.
The launch now has positive incremental profit under the stated demand assumptions.
Reconsider a phased launch while confirming the partner can deliver the quoted capacity.

title: A waste-services acquisition
prompt: A regional waste-services operator is considering buying a smaller competitor. The seller highlights strong earnings and route overlap. The buyer wants to know whether the commercial case supports the proposed price.

clarifying_facts.answer: Proceed only at no more than six times verified recurring post-action EBITDA and with acceptable customer and execution risk.
The offered amount is enterprise value; do not add a separate net-debt adjustment to this multiple.
Normalize only the disclosed items; replacement-manager compensation is necessary and recurring.
A significant customer has terminated its contract; the lost contribution is a separate change after the standalone normalization.
The stated route-cost synergy is already net of recurring delivery costs and is fully achievable from the first forecast year.
The multiple is an explicit buyer screening rule, not a claim that every asset is fairly valued at that multiple.

key_buckets: Recurring standalone earnings quality
Customer demand, retention and concentration
Incremental integration benefits and costs
Purchase terms, valuation limits and execution risk
common_gaps: Adding one-off gains to recurring earnings
Missing a necessary replacement management cost
Counting synergies while ignoring customer losses

exhibit.title: Target earnings normalization; all figures are in millions of dollars. Reported EBITDA includes the legal expense and disposal gain, but excludes the required replacement compensation.

stages.question: What is normalized annual EBITDA, in millions of dollars?

verification.method: Rebuild normalized earnings in integer dollars, reversing the expense and gain and inserting the missing recurring pay.
verification.working: Normalized EBITDA = 2 plus 0.2 minus 0.1 minus 0.15 = 39/20 million dollars, equal to 1.95 million dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Omits the missing recurring replacement compensation.
Adds the disposal gain instead of removing it.

stages.question: What commercial diligence would you prioritize before signing?
strong_ideas: Review contract renewals and termination rights
Interview major customers about service and switching risk
Map route overlap against actual customer locations
Audit the cost baseline behind proposed synergies
Assess service capacity after integration
Test customer concentration under a downside forecast
probes: Which finding could invalidate the earnings base?
How would you avoid counting the same route saving twice?

exhibit.title: Acquisition economics; all figures are in millions of dollars. Lost customer contribution is not already removed from normalized EBITDA, and verified cost synergies are fully recurring.
rows: Annual contribution lost from a terminated customer

stages.question: What enterprise-value-to-EBITDA multiple is paid after the customer loss and synergies, as an exact multiple?

verification.method: Recompute post-action earnings and purchase price in integer dollars, then reduce their ratio exactly.
verification.working: Post-loss, post-synergy EBITDA = 1.95 plus 0.3 minus 0.45 = 1.8 million dollars. Paid multiple = 12 divided by 1.8 = 20/3 times.

common_mistakes.description: Counts synergies but ignores the terminated customer.
Deducts customer loss but omits the verified recurring cost synergies.

stages.question: How does the revised multiple affect the buyer screening decision?
key_points: The current price exceeds the earnings multiple permitted by the buyer after the disclosed customer loss.
The seller headline earnings are not the right recurring denominator.
A cheaper price, contingent consideration or stronger verified earnings would be needed to reopen the case.

recommendation.question: Would you recommend buying at the stated price?
key_points: Do not approve the acquisition at the current price under the stated buyer screening rule.
Negotiate price or contingent terms linked to verified recurring customer earnings.
Continue diligence on customer concentration and route synergies.
Keep valuation discipline separate from the strategic appeal of geographic overlap.
risks_and_next_steps: Validate customer termination and replacement prospects
Confirm replacement management pay
Prove route savings without service deterioration
Review integration costs and contractual liabilities outside this earnings screen

follow_up_twist.new_fact: A signed replacement customer contract fully restores the lost annual contribution, without changing the price, synergies or other costs.
what_should_change: Recompute the paid multiple on the restored recurring earnings.
The transaction now passes the stated multiple screen.
Reopen the acquisition recommendation subject to contract quality, concentration and integration diligence.

title: Where the production line stalls
prompt: A small workshop is missing orders despite spare time in parts of the factory. Management is considering new equipment. They want help deciding where to focus and whether spending would pay off.

clarifying_facts.answer: Increase fulfilled demand and approve an improvement only if its first-year incremental net cash benefit is positive.
Every item passes through cutting, assembly and packing in that order.
Use deterministic steady-state capacity with sufficient work in progress, no scrap and no other downtime.
The upgrade exhibit shows firm paid demand rather than a market-size aspiration.
Unit contribution is after all variable operating costs; the upgrade cash cost is the only added fixed commitment.
The upgrade is available for the full first operating year; ignore taxes and working-capital changes.

key_buckets: Demand and service gap
Capacity and bottlenecks at each serial step
Improvement cost and realizable sales contribution
Implementation, quality and sustained throughput
common_gaps: Adding or averaging serial step capacities
Upgrading a non-bottleneck without changing total throughput
Assuming capacity automatically becomes paid sales

exhibit.title: Serial production steps; no scrap, downtime, buffers or other constraints. Each finished unit visits every step and there is enough work in progress to run at steady state.

stages.question: What is the maximum steady-state output, as a whole number of finished units per day?

verification.method: Enumerate whole daily output levels and require that every serial step has enough productive minutes.
verification.working: Cutting capacity = 8 times 60 divided by 4 = 120 units per day. Assembly = 480 divided by 6 = 80; packing = 480 divided by 3 = 160. The slowest step limits finished output to 80 units per day.

common_mistakes.description: Averages the separate step capacities instead of using the bottleneck.
Uses the fastest step as the finished-output limit.

stages.question: What would you try before approving a major equipment purchase?
strong_ideas: Observe assembly work to identify avoidable waits
Reduce changeover time at the bottleneck
Balance tasks across qualified operators
Check whether rework creates hidden load
Pilot a modest assembly process improvement
Confirm paid demand and delivery priorities
probes: Why might faster packing not improve finished output?
How would you verify that the bottleneck shifted after an improvement?

exhibit.title: Assembly upgrade reduces its minutes per unit to four; current and upgraded finished-output limits are shown. All added output is sold up to firm demand; no other costs, taxes or working-capital changes.
rows: Firm paid demand, units per day
One-time upgrade cash cost, thousand dollars

stages.question: What is the incremental first-year net cash benefit of the upgrade, in thousands of dollars?

verification.method: Build baseline and upgraded cash contribution separately, cap sales at demand, then compare after setup cash.
verification.working: Extra sales = minimum of 120 and 100, minus minimum of 80 and 100 = 20 units per day. Annual extra contribution = 20 times 25 times 200 = 100 thousand dollars. Net first-year benefit = 100 minus 40 = 60 thousand dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Sells every unit of extra capacity despite the demand ceiling.
Ignores the one-time upgrade cash cost.

stages.question: What limits the value of the upgraded line now?
key_points: The upgrade removes assembly as the sole old constraint.
Cutting and upgraded assembly set a higher process limit, but firm demand is lower than that limit.
The business should evaluate paid output, not value every technically available slot as a sale.

recommendation.question: Would you recommend the upgrade, and where should management focus?
key_points: Prioritize the assembly upgrade after a practical throughput trial.
The demand-capped first-year cash benefit is positive after the stated setup payment.
Verify cutting and packing can sustain the modeled upgraded flow.
Keep monitoring paid demand rather than building more capacity automatically.
risks_and_next_steps: Confirm productive minutes through observation
Check actual customer order commitments
Validate upgrade timing and quality
Measure throughput at the finished-goods boundary

follow_up_twist.new_fact: Confirmed paid demand falls to seventy units per day, with all capacities and upgrade costs unchanged.
what_should_change: Defer the upgrade at the revised demand level.
Existing capacity already covers the confirmed orders, so the purchase does not unlock extra sales.
Shift attention to demand generation or another operational problem rather than unused capacity.

title: Covering the afternoon peak
prompt: A service desk receives complaints about long afternoon waits even though mornings seem quiet. The manager wants to improve coverage without unnecessarily increasing staffing cost.

clarifying_facts.answer: Meet the stated deterministic workload and minimum coverage rules at the lowest extra daily cash cost.
Arrival and service rates are fixed for this exercise; ignore queueing variability, breaks and backlog.
All people in the staffing options are qualified for the same calls.
A minimum of seven people must remain in the morning, including the required backup coverage.
The listed redeployment and temporary staffing options are available each day without other costs.
All plans in the second exhibit cover the afternoon requirement; the remaining decision is morning feasibility and cost.

key_buckets: Demand and workload by time window
Productive staffing and service capacity
Redeployment constraints and minimum coverage
Feasible staffing costs and implementation
common_gaps: Using an average hour instead of covering the peak
Reporting total staff rather than extra staff
Choosing free redeployment while violating another coverage rule

exhibit.title: Calls and service are deterministic for this staffing exercise; no backlog, breaks or additional queueing buffer is required.

stages.question: What minimum additional afternoon staffing is needed to handle the hourly demand, as a whole number of people?

verification.method: Enumerate additional staffing levels and stop at the first that covers the stated deterministic afternoon demand.
verification.working: Afternoon staffing needed = 60 divided by 6 = 10 people. Existing afternoon staff = 8. Additional people = 2. One fewer added person would leave capacity below demand.

common_mistakes.description: Uses average morning and afternoon demand instead of covering the peak.
Reports total required staff rather than additional staff.

stages.question: What operational changes would you investigate beyond simply adding permanent headcount?
strong_ideas: Adjust shift start and end times
Redeploy qualified people between time windows
Move discretionary administration out of the peak
Improve routing to avoid repeat transfers
Review predictable sources of afternoon demand
Measure resolution time and repeat contacts by call category
probes: Which action can be tested without changing total paid hours?
What extra analysis would real-world variable arrivals require?

exhibit.title: All three plans provide the required two extra afternoon people. Staff are equally qualified, costs are daily, and the morning coverage floor is binding.

stages.question: What is the lowest extra daily cash cost that meets both coverage requirements, in dollars?

verification.method: Check plans in increasing cost order and reject each plan that fails the minimum morning coverage.
verification.working: Redeploying two costs zero but leaves only six morning staff, below seven, so it is infeasible. Hiring two costs 200 dollars. The hybrid leaves seven morning staff and costs 100 dollars, making it the least-cost feasible plan.

common_mistakes.description: Picks the cheapest plan without enforcing the morning coverage floor.
Considers only hiring both extra people and ignores feasible redeployment.

stages.question: Why is the cheapest quoted staffing option not necessarily the right option?
key_points: A plan must satisfy both afternoon demand and morning minimum coverage.
Redeploying both people solves one problem by violating another condition.
The hybrid is the least-cost feasible plan under the given rules, not simply the lowest listed cost.

recommendation.question: Which staffing plan would you use, and what would you monitor?
key_points: Use one redeployed person and one temporary afternoon person.
This covers the peak while preserving the minimum morning staffing.
Check actual call patterns and service outcomes before making the arrangement permanent.
Use a queueing and variability assessment if applying this deterministic exercise to a real service target.
risks_and_next_steps: Confirm staff qualifications and availability
Watch morning service after redeployment
Check temporary-staff reliability
Update demand and service-time estimates

follow_up_twist.new_fact: The required morning coverage floor increases to eight people; afternoon workload and all option costs stay unchanged.
what_should_change: The hybrid redeployment plan is no longer feasible.
Use the fully temporary afternoon plan among the listed options.
Reconfirm the extra budget and review whether another compliant shift design exists.

title: The largest accounts are not the best accounts
prompt: A training provider has been pursuing large corporate accounts, but delivery teams feel stretched and the founder questions whether growth is profitable. Which customers should the business prioritize?

clarifying_facts.answer: Maximize first-year incremental net contribution within the available delivery hours.
Use one full year of customer revenue and service cost, and charge acquisition cost once per new customer.
Corporate economics are a diagnostic; the quantified next campaign can choose only the listed willing Solo and Family prospects.
The campaign has one shared service-hour pool; the repeated capacity figure is not separate capacity for each segment.
Customers are indivisible, willing-customer limits are binding, and no additional cross-selling or longer-term value is assumed.
All acquisition and variable delivery costs are in the quoted net margins; fixed overhead is unchanged.

key_buckets: Segment demand and acquisition effort
First-year contribution after service and acquisition cost
Scarce delivery-hour use and feasible customer mix
Segment proposition, execution and longer-term risks
common_gaps: Ranking segments by revenue per customer alone
Applying acquisition cost once to an entire cohort
Optimizing contribution without the shared service-capacity constraint

exhibit.title: New customer cohort; every customer receives one full year of service. Acquisition cost is incurred once per new customer and all other costs are unchanged.
columns: Annual service cost per customer, dollars

stages.question: What total first-year net contribution does the corporate cohort generate, in dollars?

verification.method: Build corporate revenue, service cost and acquisition cost as three separate cohort cash ledgers.
verification.working: Corporate revenue = 20 times 600 = 12,000 dollars. Service cost = 20 times 450 = 9,000 dollars. Acquisition cost = 20 times 200 = 4,000 dollars. Net contribution = -1000 dollars.

common_mistakes.description: Ignores acquisition cost when comparing first-year customer economics.
Charges acquisition cost once for the whole cohort rather than for each new customer.

stages.question: What could explain the corporate segment economics, and how might management improve them?
strong_ideas: Check acquisition effort and sales-cycle cost
Separate standard from bespoke delivery work
Review pricing for high-service requests
Standardize content where customers accept it
Measure renewal and repeat-sales evidence before assigning lifetime value
Consider contract minimums or paid customization
probes: When could a first-year loss still be commercially justified?
How would you avoid imposing an unsupported lifetime-value assumption?

exhibit.title: Incremental next-year campaign using only Solo and Family prospects; net margins include one-off acquisition costs and all service costs. Whole customers, no other constraints, and one shared pool of hours.
rows: First-year net margin per new customer, dollars
Shared available service hours, not additive

stages.question: What is the maximum first-year net contribution the campaign can generate within the shared service capacity, in dollars?

verification.method: Enumerate every integer Family and Solo customer combination within the shared hours and demand limits.
verification.working: Family earns 70 dollars for six hours; Solo earns 20 for two. Serve 30 Family customers using 180 hours and earning 2,100 dollars, then 30 Solo using 60 hours and earning 600 dollars. Total = 2700 dollars. Exhaustive integer enumeration confirms this is optimal.

common_mistakes.description: Fills Solo demand first because each customer uses fewer hours.
Accepts all willing customers and ignores the shared hours limit.

stages.question: What is the right basis for choosing customers when delivery time is scarce?
key_points: Revenue per customer and margin per customer are incomplete decision rules.
Compare net contribution per scarce hour while respecting demand limits and whole-customer feasibility.
The verified feasible mix prioritizes Family prospects, then uses remaining hours for Solo prospects.
Integer choices should be checked because a ratio ranking is not a universal proof of optimality.

recommendation.question: What customer mix and commercial focus would you recommend?
key_points: Prioritize the verified Family and Solo mix for the capacity-constrained campaign.
Do not keep expanding Corporate accounts solely because their revenue per account is higher.
Rework Corporate pricing, acquisition cost or service design before scaling that segment.
Track actual hours and net contribution by customer cohort and test longer-term value separately.
risks_and_next_steps: Validate service hours and acquisition cost
Confirm willingness at the stated prices
Monitor delivery quality under the proposed mix
Review renewal evidence without counting it as guaranteed profit

follow_up_twist.new_fact: Family customers now require twelve service hours each rather than six, with margins, demand limits and shared capacity unchanged.
what_should_change: Recalculate the feasible mix rather than reusing the original allocation.
Solo now has the stronger contribution per scarce service hour, so prioritize it before fitting additional Family customers.
Keep whole-customer and shared-capacity constraints in the revised optimization.
